extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of social theory/sociology; scholars interested in Veblen's critique of culture and education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the standards by which Veblen describes what counts as reputable or honorific learning and speech in a leisure-class culture, and how educational branches are to be judged by economic/industrial utility. Focuses on criteria (archaism, conspicuous waste, classical learning, diction, pedagogy, athletics) used to evaluate scholarship and educational practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous waste as a test of reputability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous waste of time and money serves as evidence of reputability; the expenditure of time and effort on knowledge or pursuits that have no immediate utility signals leisure-class status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the classics and elaborate finish on goods. Veblen argues that conventional insistence on a modicum of conspicuous waste is part of reputable scholarship; such waste recommends the scholar to his audience as possessing pecuniary strength and exemption from industrial necessity. Anti-pattern: valuing purely useful knowledge as 'vulgar practicality' which is objectionable under leisure-class canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical learning/dead languages as a voucher of scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to use and understand certain dead languages is conventionally expected and serves as evidence that one has spent the requisite 'wasted' years; its absence creates a presumption of hasty or precarious learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although practically useless for most scientists, knowledge of the classics functions as a ready test of reputability. The classics are prized not for industrial utility but because they visibly conform to archaism and wasted time; they act as a credential in scholarly circles. Example: Latin/Greek study as an 'evidence of wasted time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaism/obsolete diction ('classic' English) as honorific style
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Classic' always carries connotation of wasteful and archaic; use of archaic idiom and elevated, conventionalized diction lends dignity and is proper in serious discourse—serving as a reputability marker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of archaism should match context (pulpit vs market-place). Guidance: a 'facile use' of classic idiom lends dignity to trivial talk; newer diction is seen as less proper. Anti-pattern: adopting the newest spoken forms risks loss of honorific status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of speech and orthography as readily detectable reputability tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctilious spelling and purity of speech are conspicuous, time-consuming markers of reputability: conventional English orthography is archaic and its acquisition signals leisure and cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breach of orthographic proprieties discredits a writer among those with developed taste; conformity to spelling ritual is 'indispensable to a blameless scholastic life.' Orthography is singled out as the 'first and readiest test' of reputability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminative avoidance of neologisms as honorific behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding neologisms is an honorific practice: it indicates habituation to an obsolescent idiom and association with persons of leisure-class antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoidance functions both as evidence of time spent acquiring obsolete speech and as a social signal of one's class background. Anti-pattern: rapid acceptance and use of current slang or new words undermines the honorific impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of branches of learning judged by economic/industrial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Branches of knowledge should be evaluated by how far they further 'a more facile adaptation to the economic situation of today'—i.e., their contribution to collective industrial efficiency rather than aesthetic worth alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question of educational value is cast as economic: sciences and matter-of-fact branches that make for efficiency are favored over humanities that shape tastes toward consumption and lowered industrial efficiency. Use this economic criterion when judging curricular priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanities vs sciences: effect on character and industrial efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanities (classics, traditional 'culture') tend to shape a self-centered, consumption-oriented character suited to a regime of status, whereas sciences promote impersonal, industrially useful habits of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational content by its tendency to inspire 'habitual aversion to what is merely useful' (humanities) versus cultivating recognition of causal sequence and practical proficiency (sciences). Note: humanities may have higher aesthetic value but are judged disadvantageous from an economic-efficiency standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption of student time by classical learning as an economic disservice
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical learning consumes the learner's time acquiring knowledge of no practical use except as conventional scholarly requirement, thereby lowering industrial/workmanlike attitudes and economic efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights opportunity cost: time spent on archaic learning is time not spent on useful skills. It also creates terminological difficulties in useful branches when classical terminology persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Athletics and other conspicuous pursuits as alternative reputability markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Athletics (and similar costly pursuits) function like the classics as leisure-class scholarly occupations because they require waste of time and money and display archaic, unindustrial traits; thus they rival the classics for reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in American and English schools athletics have become a rival to classics for primacy in leisure-class education because success as an athlete presumes waste and expense. Use as an observable signal of leisure-class standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindergarten/non-invidious pedagogy as disruptive to status-based discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Kindergarten methods, emphasizing non-invidious development and dexterity, favor impersonal facts and are supported by idle women of the leisure class; they promote attitudes that challenge the regime of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a criterion for assessing pedagogical methods: non-invidious, practical early education advances social adaptation to industrial life and may undermine leisure-class institutions. Example: kindergarten influence reduces emulation-based incentives and aristocratic rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and continuity of habituation legitimizes canons of taste and honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Canons of taste and judgments of honor derive legitimacy from prolonged, unbroken habituation within a race or class; the longer the habituation, the more 'legitimate' the canon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating taste or honorific judgments, consider their historical transmisson and entrenched social practice. This explains why archaic standards persist and command deference even if economically disserviceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific cognition as by-product of industrial process and social origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Science grows where industrial life requires discrimination and valuation of material forces; scientific progress is driven largely by industrious-class individuals and aberrant leisure-class scions more attuned to impersonal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an explanatory evaluative criterion: faculties and institutions that foster recognition of causal sequence are productive of useful scientific knowledge. It frames where to look for reliable methods and sources of theoretical work (outside traditional scholastic discipline).
